claims.text: Severe plastic deformation can reduce post-exposure toughness degradation in high-entropy alloys.
The intervention is intended for an as-designed high-entropy alloy that initially has the desired strength–ductility combination.
High-pressure torsion or equal-channel angular pressing can be used to impose severe plastic deformation.
Severe plastic deformation modifies grain size and dislocation density.
Grain refinement can strengthen a high-entropy alloy.
Increased dislocation interactions and multiplication can enhance alloy strength.
The proposed grain-refinement and dislocation-strengthening mechanisms will improve toughness retention after heating.
The treated alloy will retain more toughness after service-relevant heating than the untreated baseline.
The treated alloy will suffer minimal loss of strength after service-relevant heating.
The treated alloy will suffer minimal loss of ductility after service-relevant heating.
The untreated comparator should have the same composition as the treated alloy.
The untreated comparator should have the same processing history as the severely plastically deformed alloy.
The proposed thermal-exposure boundary is 473 K to 1073 K for up to several hours.
The stated loading boundary is uniaxial tensile or compressive loading.
Grain growth and precipitation during heating may alter the effect of severe plastic deformation.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing post-exposure toughness, grain size, dislocation density, strength, and ductility between treated and untreated specimens.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in toughness retention would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: An untreated baseline cannot literally have the same complete processing history as a specimen subjected to severe plastic deformation. The baseline should instead share the same processing history up to, but excluding, the intervention.
The loading boundary permits only uniaxial tensile or compressive loading, whereas the proposed primary toughness measurement is Charpy impact energy, which uses dynamic impact loading.
